prompt: I'm VP of Engineering at Northwind Freight, about 60 people. We have to ship a rebuilt billing system by 15 April 2027 because our largest contract requires it. I'm choosing between hiring two senior engineers (roughly $430k combined loaded annual cost, 3 to 4 months to hire, then about 6 weeks of ramp) or contracting Brightline Studio for six months at about $145k per month. My current leaning is the agency because it's faster to start. I'm assuming the scope stays roughly where it is today, about 9 engineer-months of work. What I don't know is whether Brightline can staff people with real payments experience, or whether we'd have meaningful work for two senior hires after April. I need to tell our CEO, Jane, by Friday 23 October. Please give me a recommendation and also stress test my leaning toward the agency, including what I might be underweighting.

I run product at Acme Metrics, a B2B analytics SaaS with 1,200 customers and $14M ARR. We haven't raised prices in 30 months and want a 15 percent increase. The question is whether to apply it to everyone at renewal or only to new customers. Finance estimates the full increase adds about $1.6M ARR if churn doesn't change, versus about $350k from new customers only over the next year. I'm assuming churn rises by no more than 2 points if we touch existing accounts, but that's a guess based on one old price test with 40 accounts. I don't know how our top 30 accounts, about 38 percent of revenue, will react. The decision goes to our exec team on 29 October and the increase would start with January renewals. I'd like a recommendation and a hard challenge to my current leaning, which is to raise for everyone. This is for our CEO, Ravi.

I'm the head of platform at Tidewater Health, a 120-person company. We self-host our main relational database on a cluster run by three engineers. The contract for our hosting and support add-ons renews on 30 November, and the vendor wants a 3-year commitment at $210k per year. A managed database service quoted us about $290k per year, plus an estimated 2 to 3 months of migration work with a cutover window that needs scheduled downtime. I'm assuming we'd reassign about one engineer's time to other work after migration. I don't know whether the managed service can meet our compliance audit requirements for data residency, because their answer is due in two weeks. I need to tell our CTO, Maya, by 7 November. Please give me a recommendation and a stress test of my current leaning, which is to stay self-hosted and sign a 1-year renewal if the vendor allows it.

I'm the founder of Lumen Forms, a 25-person startup with $3.2M ARR selling form and survey software. A smaller competitor, Pebble Surveys, has offered to sell us its customer list (about 700 paying accounts, roughly $900k ARR) and its product for $2.1M, half in cash and half in stock. Pebble has the offline-data-collection feature we lack. Building it ourselves would take about 4 engineers for 5 months by my estimate. I'm assuming at least 60 percent of their customers would stay after a migration. I don't know how much of their codebase is usable, and our lawyer hasn't finished diligence on their contracts. Pebble wants an answer by 6 November, and our board meets on 3 November. I want a recommendation and a stress test of my current leaning, which is to build rather than buy. This is going to the board.

I'm the product manager for Kestrel, a scheduling app for clinics that we plan to launch on 17 November. Beta with 35 clinics turned up problems: about 4 percent of appointment syncs fail silently, and 9 of 35 beta clinics rated onboarding as confusing. Engineering says a fix needs about 4 weeks, so launch would move to mid-December. Marketing already has a conference booth booked for 18 to 20 November and a press embargo lifting on the 17th. I'm assuming most clinics won't notice the sync failures in their first month, but I'm not confident in that. I don't know if the failures cluster in one calendar integration or are spread out. I need to decide with our COO, Priya, by Monday 20 October. Please give me a recommendation and stress test my leaning, which is to delay by one month.

I'm an engineering director at Corvid Logistics, about 200 people. Our internal routing library cuts delivery-planning compute time by roughly 30 percent compared with off-the-shelf options, and it's one reason we win some bids. A few engineers want to open-source it for hiring brand and outside contributions. Our CTO, Samir, wants a decision at the leadership meeting on 5 November. I'm assuming competitors would need at least a year to build something equivalent even with our code, but I haven't tested that. I don't know whether the library has any third-party license entanglements, and legal won't finish review until late October. Maintaining it publicly would probably take about 0.5 engineer of ongoing time. I'd like a recommendation and a stress test of my current leaning, which is to keep it internal for now. The write-up goes to Samir and the other directors.

I'm general manager of the Field Notes product line at Acme Media, a notebook and planner app we've run for 7 years. It has 48,000 active users and a very loyal community, but it loses about $380k a year and takes 6 of our 90 employees. The company would like to focus on its core subscription product. I'm assuming that about a third of Field Notes users would move to our main product if we offered a migration path, though I have no data to back that up. I don't know how much the brand goodwill affects renewals in our core product. The CEO, Dana, wants my recommendation by 31 October, and any shutdown would need to be announced before the end of the year to give users 6 months of notice. Please give me a recommendation and stress test my leaning, which is to sunset it.

I'm the infrastructure lead at Basalt Games, 85 employees. Our cloud bill is about $2.4M a year with our current provider. A competing provider has quoted a package that would cut it by roughly 20 percent, around $480k a year, with committed spend over 3 years. Migration is estimated at 5 months of work from 4 engineers, and we have a major game season launching on 1 March that I don't want to put at risk. I'm assuming the new provider's performance in our key regions will match the current one, but we have only run a two-week pilot. I don't know what egress fees we'd pay during the move, or whether our current provider would offer a counter-discount. The quote expires 14 November. I need to give a recommendation to our CFO, Elena, by 7 November. Please recommend, and stress test my leaning to stay put.

I'm an engineering manager at Fernhill Software, 70 engineers. We're forming a new 6-person team for our payments integrations starting 1 December, and I need to name its lead by 24 October. The obvious candidate is Tomas, our top performer, who shipped our two biggest projects this year and is well regarded by customers. He's also abrasive: two engineers have complained to HR in the past 12 months about being dismissed in code reviews, and one transferred out. He has asked for the role and says he'll leave if passed over. I'm assuming he can improve with coaching, but I've only seen limited evidence. I don't know how the 6 prospective team members would respond, as I haven't asked them. The decision is mine, with sign-off from our VP, Aisha. Please give me a recommendation and a stress test of my leaning, which is to promote him with a coaching plan.

I'm the head of product at Quillon, a 150-person workflow software company. Our biggest customer, Harbor Group, is 11 percent of revenue ($2.9M ARR) and has asked for a custom approval-routing feature. Their renewal is on 15 January, and they've implied it depends on this. Engineering estimates it would take most of one 8-person team's capacity for a quarter, displacing a self-serve onboarding project that we expect to lift trial conversion by 10 to 15 percent. I'm assuming we could generalize about half of the custom feature for other customers, but I haven't validated that with anyone else. I don't know whether Harbor would really walk or is negotiating. I need to give our CEO, Marcus, an answer by Wednesday 22 October. I'd like a recommendation and a stress test of my current leaning, which is to accept the request.
